title: Coexistence of Griffiths phase and superparamagnetic-like behavior in La-doped antiferromagnetic CaMnO3
authors: Koustav Pal, Shuvendu Ghosh, N. N. S. V. Rama Raju, Chitrada Prasad, Kalipada Das, I. Das
abstract: The coexistence of a Griffiths phase and superparamagnetic-like short range interaction in a single-phase homogeneous manganite is of particular interest because it reveals multiple levels of magnetic clustering generated by disorder and competing exchange interactions. In bulk $\mathrm{La}_{0.19}\mathrm{Ca}_{0.81}\mathrm{MnO}_{3}$, this unusual magnetic state develops in the antiferromagnetic regime, where A-site disorder strongly modifies the local magnetic landscape. Rietveld analysis confirms a single-phase orthorhombic structure, while magnetic measurements establish a Griffiths phase below $T_{\mathrm{G}} = 280\text{ K}$ through the deviation from Curie-Weiss behavior. Superparamagnetic-like behavior persisting from 280 to 370 K further indicates that isolated magnetic clusters remain stable well into the nominally paramagnetic region. The presence of both phenomena highlights the crucial role of disorder-induced exchange randomness in stabilizing complex magnetic states in correlated perovskite oxides.
summary: This work investigates the complex magnetic behavior of $\text{La}_{0.19}\text{Ca}_{0.81}\text{MnO}_3$, confirming its single-phase orthorhombic structure. By analyzing magnetic susceptibility and entropy changes, the authors demonstrate the coexistence of a Griffiths phase and superparamagnetic behavior. This highlights that disorder-induced randomness is a key factor in stabilizing intricate magnetic states in correlated perovskite oxides.
main_problem: The study investigates the coexistence of a Griffiths phase and superparamagnetic-like behavior in a single-phase, homogeneous manganite, revealing multiple levels of magnetic clustering driven by disorder and competing interactions.
main_result: The material exhibits both a Griffiths phase below 280 K and superparamagnetic-like behavior up to 370 K, confirming the crucial role of disorder-induced exchange randomness in stabilizing complex magnetic states.
method: The research combines structural characterization (XRD, SEM-EDS) with detailed magnetic measurements (ZFC/FC, magnetic entropy change analysis) to diagnose the magnetic transitions.
model_or_system: The physical system is bulk $\text{La}_{0.19}\text{Ca}_{0.81}\text{MnO}_3$, an A-site doped antiferromagnetic manganite whose magnetism is governed by competing Double Exchange and Superexchange interactions.
key_observables: Deviation from Curie-Weiss behavior below $T_G = 280 \text{ K}$, superparamagnetic behavior between 280 K and 370 K, and the magnetic entropy change $\text{-}\Delta S_M(T, H)$.
important_parameters: Doping concentration ($\text{La}_{0.19}\text{Ca}_{0.81}$), transition temperatures ($T_G \approx 280 \text{ K}$, $T_N \approx 210 \text{ K}$), and the field exponent $n$ used for scaling analysis.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed magnetic phenomena are primarily driven by disorder-induced exchange randomness, allowing for the interpretation of the system's magnetic state via scaling laws.
figures_summary: Figures show XRD patterns confirming the single-phase orthorhombic structure, and magnetic measurements illustrate the temperature dependence of magnetization, the peak in $\text{-}\Delta S_M(T)$, and the evolution of the field exponent $n$ across different temperature regimes.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of structural confirmation (XRD/EDS) followed by detailed magnetic characterization. The magnetic analysis progresses by examining the temperature dependence of magnetization and then employing the magnetic entropy change and field exponent scaling to delineate distinct magnetic regimes (PM $\to$ SPM $\to$ GP $\to$ AFM).
why_interesting: The study provides a clear experimental demonstration of how quenched disorder can stabilize complex magnetic states (like the Griffiths phase) in correlated oxides, offering insights into magnetic frustration beyond simple mean-field models.
